vignette:
She is 42, European, married, and has spent most of her adult life in demanding, high-risk environments, first as a combat pilot and later as a relief worker in a war zone. She carries herself with the clipped precision of someone accustomed to command checklists and split-second decisions, but in session it becomes clear that her body has not fully left the country where the trauma occurred. She describes the deployment as a place where every day felt narrowly survivable, where the line between helping and being harmed was constantly shifting.

She had gone there under the conviction that competence would protect her. Her military background made her comfortable with structure, with threat assessments, with the logic of staying calm while others panicked. As part of the relief effort, she moved supplies, coordinated evacuations, and traveled between damaged clinics and temporary distribution sites. The work mattered to her. She remembers the faces of children waiting in lines, the exhausted staff who kept working after nights of shelling, the way the air itself seemed to vibrate with fear. At first, she tells herself she can function there the way she has functioned in other dangerous settings. She is careful, alert, efficient.

The event that changes everything happens on an ordinary afternoon, which she remembers as part of what makes it unbearable. She is in transit with a convoy when the road is struck. There is a flash, then sound catches up all at once: metal tearing, shouting, the abrupt silence after impact. She feels herself thrown against the seat and then is immediately moving, opening doors, pulling people out, scanning for blood, for another blast, for the next thing that will kill them. A colleague is badly injured. Someone is crying for a family member. She does not describe the scene with dramatic language; instead, she recalls the details in a flat, exact way, as if naming them precisely will keep them from returning. What stays with her is the helplessness of being trained for emergencies while confronted with a chaos she cannot control. She says that in the moment she is not thinking of herself at all, only of getting others out alive.

Afterward, she keeps working. She helps with evacuation and triage, speaks in the firm, practical voice she has used in cockpits and command rooms, and notices that her hands shake only when she is alone. The real collapse comes later, once she is back in safer conditions and expected to “recover.” Instead, she finds that her mind keeps reentering the convoy, replaying the sound of the explosion, the sensation of heat, the image of her colleague on the ground. She wakes from dreams with her heart pounding, already disoriented, sometimes reaching for her phone before she is fully awake, as if there is something she must coordinate before dawn. Loud noises make her jerk hard enough to spill coffee or drop a dish. She starts sitting with her back to walls, counting exits, scanning rooms without meaning to. She notices how she tenses when a car backfires, how she flinches when a helicopter passes overhead, how her stomach drops at the smell of diesel because it carries her back.

Her marriage becomes more strained in the months that follow. Her husband tells her she is distant, always checking windows, answering questions as though she is elsewhere. She loves him, but she cannot easily tolerate touch when she is startled, and she becomes irritable over small things she would once have brushed aside. She is ashamed of how quickly anger rises in her now, how often she feels on edge, as if her body is permanently braced for impact. She has stopped reading news from the region because even brief updates leave her flooded with dread and helplessness. She avoids certain routes in the city because construction noise reminds her too much of the convoy. She turns down invitations, not because she wants to be alone, but because she cannot predict what will set her off.

At work, she is still competent, but it costs her more. As a pilot, she has always relied on discipline, yet she now catches herself overchecking instruments, struggling to settle after missions or training flights. She can hide a great deal in a professional setting, but she feels the effort in her bones. Her concentration slips. She rereads messages. She loses track of conversations when a sound from outside triggers a sudden wash of memory. The part of her that used to move toward risk with confidence now seems split from the part that stays hyperalert and exhausted.

Even so, there are moments when she can speak about the people she helped, and in those moments her face softens. She holds onto the belief that the work meant something, even as she grieves what it cost her. She is not yet at ease in ordinary life, but she is trying to understand why the war remains so present inside her, long after she has left it behind.
